newsitem.title: THAILAND: Khmer Rouge relax at ancient border temple.
newsitem.headline: Khmer Rouge relax at ancient border temple.

text.p: Khmer Rouge guerrillas holding an ancient mountain-top temple on the Thai-Cambodian border seem unusually relaxed of late, apparently due to hopes a deal ending their war with the Cambodian government is imminent.
Thai traders said they too were looking forward to peace and the reopening to tourists of the ruins of the ancient Khmer temple of Preah Vihear.
Thai military sources on the border, based on a mountain-top several hundred metres (yards) from the Cambodian temple, said unusual signs have been coming from their Khmer Rouge neighbours lately.
"Sometimes we even hear them singing songs over their field radios," said one Thai soldier late on Saturday. "They seem so relaxed".
Looking through binoculars from the Thai base, dozens of Khmer Rouge guerrillas could be seen strolling around the ruins.
None was carrying a gun and while some were dressed in their distinctive Chinese-supplied green uniforms, others were shirtless or simply dressed in Cambodian-style sarongs.

Political analysts in Phnom Penh say the Khmer Rouge guerrilla group appears to be unravelling following bloody infighting among its top leaders and the capture of the hated Pol Pot by his former colleagues.

Pol Pot was leader of the Khmer Rouge's bloody "killing fields" regime from 1975-79. After the Khmer Rouge regime was overthrown by a Vietnamese invasion, it fought the Hanoi-installed government until a peace treaty was signed in 1991. But the Khmer Rouge later reneged on the treaty and had been fighting Cambodia's coalition government.
Cambodia's First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh has been negotiating with the rebels in an effort to get them to give up their fight and join with the government.
News of the talks appears to have reached both sides of the border at Preah Vihear.
"We heard that the Khmer Rouge will make a deal with the government in the near future," said a Thai army officer.
"Negotiations to reopen the temple for tourists are already underway," he said.
Thai traders and business officials are also optimistic that the fighting will soon end and the only armies at the temple in future will be armies of tourists.
"We've been told the temple is set to reopen soon. That's good news," said souvenir vendor Thiongrein Fuihutha, at his stall at the base of the mountain on the Thai side of the border.
Chaval Mahasuvirachai, president of the chamber of commerce in Thailand's Si Sa Khet province, said he felt the Khmer Rouge were nearly finished, and that could only be good for business.
"The Khmer Rouge is about to come to an end and I hope that in the near future we can talk with the Cambodian government to reopen the temple as a tourist spot," Chaval told Reuters.

The temple, set on the edge of the Dang Raek escarpment overlooking the north Cambodian plain, was captured by the Khmer Rouge in early 1993. Some 300 guerrillas have held off intermittent government attempts to take it back since then.

Access to the ruined temple, built around the same time as the famed Angkor Wat temple complex, is extremely difficult from the Cambodian side of the border where there is a steep cliff, but an easy walk from the Thai side.
